overview.title: 📖 Overview: Testimony, Repetition, and the Pace of Eating
overview.subtitle: Keritot 12a–12b
overview.hebrewSource: אָדָם נֶאֱמָן עַל עַצְמוֹ יוֹתֵר מִמֵּאָה אִישׁ
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf works through the practical edges of the previous mishna on witnesses and sin offerings: why the Rabbis exempt someone who denies two witnesses' testimony, whether their reasoning is a broad credibility principle or a narrower 'better claim' (miggo) logic, and how that choice plays out differently for old versus new ritual impurity. Several Sages then identify additional cases where even Rabbi Meir concedes to the Rabbis, each turning on a hidden alternative claim the accused could have made. The Gemara then returns to the mishna's rules about eating forbidden substances — when two olive-bulks in one lapse of awareness combine into one liability, when eating from separate dishes creates two liabilities instead, and finally, in a new mishna, exactly how much time a person may take to eat a forbidden olive-bulk and still be liable.

slides.title: 🤔 A Person's Word Against Witnesses
slides.subtitle: Why do the Rabbis exempt someone who denies two witnesses' testimony?

lines.speaker: R' Meir
lines.text: A fortiori: if two witnesses can convict someone of a capital crime, surely they can obligate him in a mere offering!

lines.speaker: The Rabbis
lines.text: Not necessarily — but why exactly? Two theories: either 'a person is more credible about himself than a hundred witnesses,' or simply that he has a better claim available (miggo) — he could have said 'I did it intentionally' and been exempt, so his weaker denial is believed too.

lines.speaker: Testing the theories
lines.text: Applied to old ritual impurity (witnesses: 'you were impure yesterday'): under the miggo theory he's exempt, since he could claim 'I immersed since then.' Applied to new impurity (witnesses: 'you just became impure'): the miggo theory would make him liable, since no such claim is available.

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: A baraita confirms the broader credibility principle: even for new impurity, the Rabbis hold he is simply more believable than the witnesses. Rav Naḥman rules the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda (=the Rabbis' view) on this.

callout.label: Caveat:
callout.text: Rav Yosef limits this: he is believed only for his own purposes (to avoid an offering), not to declare himself pure in matters affecting others.

slides.title: 🙅 Where Even Rabbi Meir Concedes
slides.subtitle: In each case, a hidden 'better claim' persuades even Rabbi Meir that a denial is credible
rows: 'I did not complete the act' (Reish Lakish) — since only completed intercourse creates liability
'I had my vow dissolved by a halakhic authority' (Rav Sheshet) — permitting contact otherwise forbidden
'I did not intend to testify' (Abaye) — since only an intentional false oath of testimony creates liability
Whenever a milder, believable alternative claim exists, even Rabbi Meir agrees the person's denial is credible against two witnesses

callout.label: The exception that proves the rule:
callout.text: Ravina shows why plain ritual impurity from direct contact is different — there, no alternative claim can explain away 'I did not become impure' once witnesses saw the contact itself.

slides.title: 🍽️ One Lapse, One Offering — Unless the Dishes Divide It
slides.subtitle: The mishna's rule on eating forbidden fat twice, and how 'separate dishes' complicates it

nodes.content: 🧀 Ate an olive-bulk of forbidden fat, then another olive-bulk, in one lapse of awareness → only one sin offering (same lapse = same liability)
❓ Rabbi Zeira: but he ate two full olive-bulks — why just one offering? Abaye: separate lapses of awareness divide liability, not separate bites within one lapse
🍲 Two half-olive-bulks eaten from two different dishes, same food type: Reish Lakish (name of bar Tutini) — per Rabbi Yehoshua, this creates two separate transgressions, hence liability

⚖️ But could the same rule work as a leniency (two dishes of two DIFFERENT foods, still exempting him from combining to a full measure)? The mishna's phrasing shows Rabbi Yehoshua's 'dishes divide' rule applies to both stringency and leniency
✅ Ravina's alternative for the 'one dish' case: it involves intervening awareness between two half-measures — valid under Rabban Gamliel's view that awareness doesn't interrupt sub-measure eating

callout.label: Underlying theme:
callout.text: Whether two partial acts combine into liability depends on precise technical dividers — the lapse of awareness, and even the dish the food was served on.

slides.title: ⏱️ How Long Counts As 'Eating'?
slides.subtitle: A new mishna: the maximum time allowed to consume a forbidden olive-bulk

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rabbi Meir: the time allowed is as long as it takes to eat roasted grain — kernel by kernel
2️⃣ The Rabbis: liability requires eating the whole olive-bulk within the longer time it takes to eat a half-loaf of bread (kdei achilat pras)

3️⃣ Gemara's dilemma: is Rabbi Meir's standard a stringency (liable even if it takes all day, so long as there's no gap) or a leniency (liable only if eaten with zero interruption, even within the shorter pras-window)?
4️⃣ Resolved from the Rabbis' own phrasing — 'from beginning to end' — showing the debate is about total elapsed time, not about interruptions

callout.label: Why it matters:
callout.text: This time-window determines whether scattered small bites of a forbidden food ever combine into a liable olive-bulk.

slides.title: 📝 No Awareness for a Half-Measure
slides.subtitle: Rabban Gamliel's rule lets two half-measures combine even across an interruption of awareness
slides.label: The principle:
slides.text: Ravina explains a puzzling case in the mishna — eating two half-olive-bulks of the same forbidden food from the same dish, which seems obviously liable — by positing that the person actually became briefly aware of his sin between the two half-bites. Whether that awareness breaks the chain depends on a known dispute, drawn from the parallel case of writing two letters on Shabbat in two lapses: Rabban Gamliel holds there is no legal 'awareness' for a mere half-measure, so the two half-bulks still combine into one liability; the Rabbis hold awareness of even a half-measure does divide the acts, so no liability results.

summary.principle: Liability for a sin offering turns on fine distinctions — whether a denial has a believable alternative explanation, whether acts occurred in one lapse of awareness or separate dishes, and precisely how much time and interruption is allowed while eating a forbidden olive-bulk.

flowSteps.content: 🤔 The Rabbis exempt a denial against two witnesses because a person is more credible about himself than many witnesses
🙅 Even Rabbi Meir concedes wherever a milder alternative claim could explain the denial
🍽️ One lapse of awareness yields one offering; separate dishes can still divide liability as a stringency

columns.content: ⏱️ Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis dispute how much elapsed time still counts as one continuous act of eating
📝 Rabban Gamliel: no legal 'awareness' exists for a mere half-measure, so half-bulks still combine

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: the Torah's liability rules track precise technical boundaries — of time, awareness, and available alternative claims — never a general impression of guilt

quiz.q: According to the version of the debate resolved by a baraita, why do the Rabbis (per Rabbi Yehuda's formulation) hold that a person's denial is credible even against two witnesses?
o: Because two witnesses are never reliable
Because a person is deemed more credible about himself than the testimony of a hundred people
Because witnesses can never testify about sin offerings
Because denial always exempts regardless of witnesses
quiz.e: The baraita confirms the Rabbis' reasoning as a broad credibility principle — a person is more believable about his own status than the testimony of many witnesses — rather than merely a narrower 'better claim' (miggo) argument.

quiz.q: According to Reish Lakish, why does even Rabbi Meir concede that a denial is credible when two witnesses accuse someone of relations with an espoused maidservant?
o: Because maidservants cannot testify
Because he could have claimed 'I did not complete the act,' which would exempt him even if true
Because the case never involves an offering
Because Rabbi Meir has no opinion on this case
quiz.e: Reish Lakish explains that since only a completed act of intercourse creates liability for this offering, the accused's denial can be understood as the believable claim that he only began but did not complete the act — a claim even Rabbi Meir accepts.

quiz.q: According to Abaye's answer to Rabbi Zeira, why is one liable to only one sin offering for eating two olive-bulks of forbidden fat, when clearly he ate two full measures?
o: Because forbidden fat has no minimum measure
Because both olive-bulks were eaten within a single lapse of awareness, and only separate lapses divide liability
Because he ate them from the same dish
Because forbidden fat is treated leniently
quiz.e: Abaye explains that liability for separate sin offerings is divided by separate lapses of awareness (as derived from Leviticus 4:28), not by the mere quantity of food eaten within one lapse.

quiz.q: According to the mishna, what is the key difference between Rabbi Meir's and the Rabbis' standards for how much time one may take to eat a forbidden olive-bulk?
o: Rabbi Meir allows any amount of time; the Rabbis require immediate consumption
Rabbi Meir measures by the pace of eating roasted grain kernel by kernel; the Rabbis allow the longer time it takes to eat a half-loaf of bread
There is no actual difference between them
The Rabbis are always more lenient than Rabbi Meir
quiz.e: Rabbi Meir's standard is the (shorter) pace of eating roasted grain one kernel at a time, while the Rabbis allow the longer duration of eating a half-loaf (peras) of bread.

quiz.q: According to Rabban Gamliel's principle 'there is no awareness for a half-measure,' what is the practical result when someone eats a half-olive-bulk, becomes briefly aware of his sin, and then eats another half-olive-bulk of the same food?
o: The two half-measures never combine into liability
The two half-measures still combine into one liability, since a mere half-measure's worth of awareness does not divide the acts
He is liable to two separate offerings
He is entirely exempt regardless of the amounts
quiz.e: Rabban Gamliel holds that legal 'awareness' does not apply to a mere half-measure, so the intervening awareness does not prevent the two half-olive-bulks from combining into a single liability, unlike the Rabbis' opposing view.
